newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turks report foreign forces near Kurd enclave.
newsitem.headline: Turks report foreign forces near Kurd enclave.

text.p: Turkey's state-run Anatolian news agency said on Wednesday that Syria, Iraq and Iran had built up their forces near the borders of a Kurdish enclave in northern Iraq where Turkish troops are fighting Kurdish rebels.

Anatolian quoted unnamed sources as saying the buildup was believed to be part of an effort by the three countries to provide shelter within their borders to Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) rebels fleeing the Turkish air and ground assault.
"Syria, the country which gives the biggest support to the (PKK) separatist organisation, has built up troops at the northern Iraq border using the excuse of a military exercise," Anatolian said.
It said Iran and Iraq had also built up forces around the Kurdish territory, carved out of northern Iraq as a "safe haven" for the Kurds by the Western alliance after the Gulf War.

Damascus declined to comment on the reports but said Ankara's incursion in Iraq, now in its eighth day, showed bad intentions against its neighbours. There was no immediate response from Iraq or Iran.

Pro-PKK MED-TV told Reuters that about 50 Iraqi tanks had moved closer to the Mosul road, on the edge of the Kurdish enclave where Turkish soldiers had set up checkpoints. However, the Iraqi armour remained in government territory, it said.
MED-TV, based in Belgium, also reported that Syria had begun war games to the south of its border with the Iraqi Kurdish enclave three days ago.
"Turkey's incursion inside Iraqi territory reflects bad intentions by the Turkish authorities against their neighbours," a senior Syrian official told Reuters in Damascus.
The anti-Baghdad Iraqi National Congress said it had received reports from the area of a buildup by Iranian and Iraqi forces on the borders of the "safe haven".
A spokesman for the INC, based in London, said Iranian revolutionary guards had been sent to the border regions.

Iraqi republican guards, backed by tanks, were gathered between the government city of Mosul and Dohuk, inside the enclave, near the Fayda checkpoint which separates the Kurdish region from the rest of Iraq, the INC said.
More than 10,000 Turkish troops last week began a major cross-border operation in pursuit of PKK separatists who use northern Iraq as a base to launch raids into southeast Turkey.
Turkey showed no signs of letting up on the operation on Wednesday, ferrying in more troops and supplies. Military sources say more than 1,300 PKK rebels have been killed so far.
PKK sources, however, say that figure is grossly inflated.
Ankara and its Iraqi Kurdish allies have denied reporters access to the region since the start of the incursion, making confirmation of the size and scope of the operation impossible.
The incursion has drawn criticism from Ankara's Western allies, the United Nations as well as countries in the region.
Syria, which earlier described the cross-border operation as an "invasion", drew a rebuke from the Turkish Foreign Ministry on Wednesday.
"Syria is supporting the PKK, cursed by all the world as a terrorist organisation, and is using terrorism as a tool in its foreign policy," spokesman Omer Akbel told reporters.
